transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I guess what brings me in is that my eating has just gotten so off lately. Like, some days I barely get down a cup of coffee and a granola bar before I clock in for my shift. I work as a healthcare support worker, and honestly, the coffee in our breakroom has been terrible ever since administration switched suppliers last month. It’s this cheap dark roast that just tastes like burnt dirt. I don't know who makes these purchasing decisions, probably someone in corporate who never even steps foot on our floor... but, um, anyway, yeah, I'm barely eating. 

And I noticed my scrubs have been hanging really loose on me lately, even though I'm not trying to lose weight at all. Which is annoying because I just bought these new ones with the extra cargo pockets on the thigh—you really need those pockets for all the tape and extra supplies when you're doing patient transport—and now they just sag right off my waist. The drawstring is pulled as tight as it goes.
Are you avoiding food or eating less because you are worried about gaining weight?

No, no, not at all. Like I said, I'm definitely not trying to lose weight. I just... I don't know, I just don't have the appetite for it. I look at food and it just seems like too much effort to even chew it. Which is weird because I used to love stopping by this little diner near the hospital after a long shift. They make this incredible meatloaf—like, real homestyle meatloaf with the crispy edges and the thick brown gravy. The waitress there, Shirley, she always knows exactly how I like my potatoes, too. Mashed, but with the skins still mixed in. She's been working there for, gosh, must be fifteen years. Her daughter actually just graduated from nursing school, which is great, because we really need more nurses on our floor. The staffing ratios have been a nightmare lately. But yeah, no... I'm not worried about gaining weight. I just barely eat my coffee and a granola bar, and that's it. And then my scrubs are just falling off me.
Aside from your appetite, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless lately?

Yeah, I guess you could say that. It's... well, most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the day is already ruined before I even put on my badge. It's just this weight in my chest. And speaking of my badge, the clip on it broke last week, the retractable kind? I had to use a safety pin to attach it to my scrubs, which is just a hazard waiting to happen when you're helping patients out of bed. I put in a request for a new one with HR, but you know how they are. They said it takes three to five business days to process a replacement, but with the holiday weekend coming up, who knows when I'll actually get it. My friend Gary in maintenance said he waited two weeks for his. Two weeks! Just to get a piece of plastic with a string in it. But, um, yeah, I just feel really down and heavy most days.
Have you ever felt this way, or experienced a period of feeling this down and having such a low appetite, at any point in your life before now?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days, sure, but nothing like this where I just... where I don't even want to eat and everything feels so heavy. I've always been a pretty steady guy. Like, even when they renovated the west wing of the hospital and we had to detour all the transport beds through the basement tunnels. Those tunnels are so creepy, by the way. The fluorescent lights flicker constantly, and there's this one pipe near the old laundry chute that makes a hissing sound every time you walk past it. I told Gary about it—he's the maintenance guy I mentioned earlier—and he said it's just steam pressure, but honestly, it sounds like a snake. A really big, angry snake. And the floors down there are always slightly damp, which makes the wheels on the transport chairs squeak. It drives me crazy. I tried spraying WD-40 on one of the chairs once, but my supervisor caught me and said it wasn't protocol. Protocol! Like we have a protocol for squeaky wheels in a damp, creepy basement. But yeah, no, I've never felt this down before. This is all new.
Aside from the changes in your appetite and feeling down, have you noticed that you've lost interest or pleasure in doing the things you used to enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, I have. I used to love going for runs in Van Cortlandt Park, you know? Taking my camera out, getting some good shots of the trees, maybe meeting up with a few buddies to play chess. But now... I just tell myself there's no point. I end up just sitting at home, scrolling on my phone or staring at my budget spreadsheet. And speaking of the budget, the price of groceries has just gotten insane. I was at the store the other day just to get coffee, right? Because like I said, that's all I'm really having. And a regular bag of the store-brand coffee was almost nine dollars. Nine dollars! I remember when you could get a premium roast for that much. And don't even get me started on eggs. I don't eat them right now, but I saw the price tag and nearly had a heart attack. The cashier—I think her name tag said Brenda—she was telling me that people have been complaining all week. She looked exhausted, honestly. Being on your feet all day dealing with angry customers... it's a lot like being at the hospital, really. People take out their frustrations on the person right in front of them, even if it's not their fault. Like this one patient we had in room 412 last month... he threw his remote at the TV because the sports channel was blacked out. But anyway... yeah, I just don't have the energy or care to do the things I used to like. Just sit at home.
Have you noticed that your movements or speech have slowed down, or do you feel so restless that you find it hard to sit still?

It's... it's kind of both, I think. Like, at work, sometimes I can't stop moving. I'll just pace around the supply area, opening the same drawers over and over, checking the gauze and the tape. And speaking of tape, the hospital just switched suppliers for the medical tape, and this new stuff is terrible. It doesn't stick to anything. I was trying to secure an IV line for a nurse the other day—Nurse Sarah, she's great, always brings donuts on Fridays, though I haven't been eating them lately—and the tape just kept peeling off the patient's skin. We had to use three pieces just to get it to hold. And the dispenser they gave us for the new tape is this cheap plastic thing that jams every time you try to tear a piece off. I spent like ten minutes just trying to fix the dispenser while Sarah was standing there waiting. It's so frustrating when they try to save a few pennies and end up making our jobs ten times harder. But then, on the flip side, sometimes I feel like I'm moving through molasses. Like, drawing up labels or just answering a patient when they call for help... it takes me twice as long as it should. My body just feels so heavy and slow. So yeah, it's like I'm either bouncing off the walls checking drawers or I can barely put one foot in front of the other.
With all of this heaviness and the feeling that everything is pointless, have you found yourself having any thoughts that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?

Well, I haven't... I haven't made any kind of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. But yeah, sometimes I do catch myself just wishing I wouldn't wake up. Like, it would just be so much easier if I could disappear, you know? Just poof, gone. No more dragging myself out of bed, no more dealing with the squeaky transport chairs. It reminds me of this magic show my uncle took me to when I was a kid. This guy, he called himself The Great Zamboni or something, he had this huge cabinet on stage. He put his assistant in there, closed the doors, spun it around, and when he opened it—she was gone. Poof. I always wondered how they did that trick. I mean, I know there's a trap door or mirrors involved. My cousin Eddie tried to explain it to me once. Eddie was always trying to figure out how things worked. He took apart his dad's lawnmower when he was twelve and couldn't put it back together. His dad was furious. They had to pay a guy fifty bucks to come fix it, and fifty bucks was a lot of money back then. Eddie ended up becoming an engineer, though, so I guess taking the lawnmower apart paid off in the end. He lives out in Seattle now. Rains a lot out there. I don't think I could handle all that rain. But yeah, I don't want to kill myself, I just... I just think about how nice it would be to just not be here anymore. Just disappear like that assistant in the cabinet.
Are you still able to perform your duties at work, or has your condition made it impossible for you to carry out your job responsibilities?

Well, it's getting harder, honestly. I'm still showing up, but... I've started making these really avoidable mistakes. Like, I'll forget where I put the clean linens or I'll need the nurses to repeat simple requests, like two or three times. It's embarrassing. I just can't seem to focus. It's like my brain is full of cotton. Which is weird, because I used to be so sharp. I was the guy everyone came to when they needed something found quickly. I remember this one time, Dr. Henderson lost his favorite pen—this fancy silver one his wife gave him for their anniversary. He was tearing the nurses' station apart looking for it. I found it in about two minutes, rolled under the edge of the computer cart. He was so relieved, he bought me a coffee the next day. A large one, too, from that cafe down the street that roasts their own beans. Their coffee is amazing, but the line is always out the door. I don't know how people have the patience to stand in line for twenty minutes just for a cup of coffee. Especially in the winter when the wind is whipping down the avenue. It cuts right through your coat. But anyway... yeah, work is tough right now. I don't even go to chess nights with my buddies anymore, or take my camera out for walks. I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with the game or even act normal around them. I feel like I'd just mess it up or say the wrong thing.
Are you still able to perform your job tasks, or has this feeling of 'cotton-brain' and the mistakes you're making caused you to stop working or require a leave of absence?

Well, I'm still working. I haven't taken a leave or anything, but... yeah, like I said, I'm making those dumb mistakes. I'll just completely blank on things, and the nurses have to tell me the same thing two or three times. It's just... I'm not myself. I've even stopped doing my normal stuff outside of work. Like, I used to go to chess nights with the guys, or take my camera out and just walk around the city, taking pictures. But I don't do any of that anymore. I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with the game, or even act normal around them, you know? Speaking of chess, my friend Gary, he's got this beautiful wooden chess set. Hand-carved pieces from Poland or somewhere. The knights actually look like real horses, not just those blocky shapes you usually see. Gary's a bit of a fanatic, honestly. He watches all these grandmaster games on YouTube. He tried to teach me the Sicilian Defense once, but there are just too many variations. It’s like trying to memorize a phone book. Remember when they used to deliver those huge Yellow Pages to your door? They were so heavy, you could use them as a doorstop. My grandma used to keep one in her kitchen and she’d press flowers in it. She had this garden full of hydrangeas... but yeah, I just... I haven't been going to chess or doing much of anything. I just feel like I can't keep up.
Has your inability to focus and the mistakes you are making led to any formal disciplinary action or warnings from your supervisor at the hospital?

No, I haven't... I haven't been written up or anything like that. No formal warnings. Brenda, my supervisor, she's been pretty patient, I guess. She just kind of sighs and helps me fix whatever I messed up. She wears these reading glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck, so she's always pulling them up and dropping them back down when she looks at the clipboard. 

It actually reminds me of my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had a chain for her glasses too, but hers was made of fake pearls. She loved pearls. She even had a pearl steering wheel cover in her car. It was this huge boat of a Buick. I remember because she gave me a ride home once when I missed the bus. It was raining so hard that day, the streets were basically rivers, and that Buick just glided right through the puddles. My dad used to have a LeSabre, same kind of floaty suspension. You'd hit a bump and the car would just bounce up and down for a mile. He loved that car. He'd spend every Sunday waxing it in the driveway... but, um... no, Brenda hasn't called me into the office or given me any disciplinary papers.

Are you still able to carry out your work responsibilities to the same standard as you did before you started feeling this way, or would you say your ability to function at work is significantly impaired?

Well, no, definitely not to the same standard. It's... it's definitely impaired. Like I was saying, I'm making those avoidable mistakes, and I just can't seem to hold onto a thought. The nurses have to repeat simple requests two or three times before it clicks. It's like I'm moving through molasses. And it's not just work, it's everything. I've completely stopped going to chess nights, and I haven't taken my camera out for a walk in weeks. I just don't trust myself to keep up with the game or act normal around the guys. 

My camera is a Nikon, actually. I saved up for six months to buy it. It’s got this incredible zoom lens, you can see the craters on the moon if the night is clear enough. I used to love going down to the harbor at night to take long exposure shots of the boats. The water looks like glass when you do that. You have to use a tripod, though, otherwise the picture comes out all blurry. I bought a really sturdy carbon fiber one. It’s super light but it doesn't shake in the wind. The wind down by the harbor can get pretty intense, especially in November. It just whips right off the water. You have to wear layers. My mom used to knit these thick wool scarves... she made me this one that was dark green, forest green, I guess you'd call it. It was so warm, but it was incredibly itchy. I could only wear it over a turtleneck... but yeah, I just... I can't do my job the way I used to. I'm definitely not functioning like normal.

Because you mentioned that you are still showing up to work and haven't received formal disciplinary action, would you say that you are still able to manage your basic daily self-care tasks, like showering, brushing your teeth, and keeping your home clean, or has your current state made even those simple things feel impossible?

Well, I... I try to keep up with it, but honestly, it's getting harder. Some days I just look at the shower and it feels like... like climbing a mountain, you know? I haven't been doing laundry as much. The pile just sits there. It's mostly scrubs anyway. I have these blue scrubs, they’re the only color they let us wear on the floor. 

I used to have this pair of scrubs that were a slightly different shade of blue, like a navy, and Brenda actually pulled me aside and told me I couldn't wear them. It was a whole big thing. The hospital has a very strict dress code policy. They even dictate the color of our shoes. They have to be solid white or solid black, no logos. I bought these white clogs once, the kind the chefs wear? They are supposed to be slip-resistant. I slipped in the cafeteria anyway, right in front of the salad bar. Dropped a whole tray of jello. Red jello, cherry flavor. It went everywhere. The janitor, Frank, he was so mad. Frank’s been there for like thirty years. He has this massive ring of keys on his belt, it jingles every time he walks down the hall. It sounds like a sleigh is coming. My uncle used to dress up as Santa every Christmas and he had bells just like that... but, um... yeah, self-care is... it's slipping. I'm just so tired all the time.

Given that you have stopped going to chess nights and taking your camera out, would you say that your symptoms have caused you to almost completely withdraw from your social life and personal interests?

Yeah, I guess you could say that. I just... I don't see the point anymore. Like I said, I stopped doing chess nights, and my camera is just gathering dust. I used to love running, too. I'd go for these long runs in Van Cortlandt Park. The trails there are really nice, especially in the fall when the leaves change. 

There's this one specific trail that loops around the back, near the old train tracks. They pulled the tracks up years ago, but you can still see the wooden ties rotting in the dirt. It's kind of sad, actually, thinking about how busy that train line used to be. My grandfather worked on the railroad, not that one, but out in Pennsylvania. He was a conductor. He had this beautiful pocket watch, gold plated, with an eagle engraved on the front. He used to let me hold it when I was a kid. It was so heavy in my hand. It ticked really loud, you could hear it from across the room if the house was quiet enough. The house was always quiet after my grandmother died. She used to bake these incredible apple pies, the whole house would smell like cinnamon and butter... 

But yeah, I don't run anymore. I just tell myself there's no point. I end up just sitting on my couch, scrolling on my phone or... or staring at my budget spreadsheet. Just looking at the numbers. It's all I seem to have the energy for.

doctor.intent: Assess the presence of psychomotor retardation or agitation to differentiate between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that your movements or speech have slowed down, or do you feel so restless that you find it hard to sit still?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: At work I either pace around the supply area checking the same drawers over and over, or I move so slowly that drawing up labels and answering a patient takes me twice as long as it should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about slowed down movements or speech, or restlessness, which directly corresponds to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer: It's... it's kind of both, I think. Like, at work, sometimes I can't stop moving. I'll just pace around the supply area, opening the same drawers over and over, checking the gauze and the tape. And speaking of tape, the hospital just switched suppliers for the medical tape, and this new stuff is terrible. It doesn't stick to anything. I was trying to secure an IV line for a nurse the other day—Nurse Sarah, she's great, always brings donuts on Fridays, though I haven't been eating them lately—and the tape just kept peeling off the patient's skin. We had to use three pieces just to get it to hold. And the dispenser they gave us for the new tape is this cheap plastic thing that jams every time you try to tear a piece off. I spent like ten minutes just trying to fix the dispenser while Sarah was standing there waiting. It's so frustrating when they try to save a few pennies and end up making our jobs ten times harder. But then, on the flip side, sometimes I feel like I'm moving through molasses. Like, drawing up labels or just answering a patient when they call for help... it takes me twice as long as it should. My body just feels so heavy and slow. So yeah, it's like I'm either bouncing off the walls checking drawers or I can barely put one foot in front of the other.

inference.note: The patient's report of psychomotor agitation (pacing, checking drawers) alongside psychomotor retardation (feeling like moving through molasses) supports a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, single episode. F32.9 is excluded as the severity is clearly indicated by the significant weight loss, loss of interest (anhedonia), and psychomotor changes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing suicidal ideation or intent to differentiate between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) major depressive episodes.
doctor.question: With all of this heaviness and the feeling that everything is pointless, have you found yourself having any thoughts that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I haven’t made a plan to hurt myself, but I catch myself wishing I just wouldn’t wake up or thinking it would be easier if I disappeared.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of life not being worth living or being better off dead, which maps directly to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer: Well, I haven't... I haven't made any kind of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. But yeah, sometimes I do catch myself just wishing I wouldn't wake up. Like, it would just be so much easier if I could disappear, you know? Just poof, gone. No more dragging myself out of bed, no more dealing with the squeaky transport chairs. It reminds me of this magic show my uncle took me to when I was a kid. This guy, he called himself The Great Zamboni or something, he had this huge cabinet on stage. He put his assistant in there, closed the doors, spun it around, and when he opened it—she was gone. Poof. I always wondered how they did that trick. I mean, I know there's a trap door or mirrors involved. My cousin Eddie tried to explain it to me once. Eddie was always trying to figure out how things worked. He took apart his dad's lawnmower when he was twelve and couldn't put it back together. His dad was furious. They had to pay a guy fifty bucks to come fix it, and fifty bucks was a lot of money back then. Eddie ended up becoming an engineer, though, so I guess taking the lawnmower apart paid off in the end. He lives out in Seattle now. Rains a lot out there. I don't think I could handle all that rain. But yeah, I don't want to kill myself, I just... I just think about how nice it would be to just not be here anymore. Just disappear like that assistant in the cabinet.

doctor.intent: Assess the severity of functional impairment to distinguish between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Are you still able to perform your duties at work, or has your condition made it impossible for you to carry out your job responsibilities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started making avoidable mistakes at work, needing coworkers to repeat simple requests, and avoiding chess nights and photography walks because I don’t trust myself to keep up or act normal.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to perform my duties at work and whether my condition has made it impossible to carry out my job responsibilities, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer: Well, it's getting harder, honestly. I'm still showing up, but... I've started making these really avoidable mistakes. Like, I'll forget where I put the clean linens or I'll need the nurses to repeat simple requests, like two or three times. It's embarrassing. I just can't seem to focus. It's like my brain is full of cotton. Which is weird, because I used to be so sharp. I was the guy everyone came to when they needed something found quickly. I remember this one time, Dr. Henderson lost his favorite pen—this fancy silver one his wife gave him for their anniversary. He was tearing the nurses' station apart looking for it. I found it in about two minutes, rolled under the edge of the computer cart. He was so relieved, he bought me a coffee the next day. A large one, too, from that cafe down the street that roasts their own beans. Their coffee is amazing, but the line is always out the door. I don't know how people have the patience to stand in line for twenty minutes just for a cup of coffee. Especially in the winter when the wind is whipping down the avenue. It cuts right through your coat. But anyway... yeah, work is tough right now. I don't even go to chess nights with my buddies anymore, or take my camera out for walks. I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with the game or even act normal around them. I feel like I'd just mess it up or say the wrong thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's impairment is severe enough to meet the criteria for F32.2 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, severe without psychotic symptoms) by assessing the degree of functional impairment.
doctor.question: Are you still able to perform your job tasks, or has this feeling of 'cotton-brain' and the mistakes you're making caused you to stop working or require a leave of absence?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started making avoidable mistakes at work, needing coworkers to repeat simple requests, and avoiding chess nights and photography walks because I don’t trust myself to keep up or act normal.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question regarding the extent of my functional impairment at work, specifically whether I have had to stop working or take a leave of absence due to my symptoms.

patient.answer: Well, I'm still working. I haven't taken a leave or anything, but... yeah, like I said, I'm making those dumb mistakes. I'll just completely blank on things, and the nurses have to tell me the same thing two or three times. It's just... I'm not myself. I've even stopped doing my normal stuff outside of work. Like, I used to go to chess nights with the guys, or take my camera out and just walk around the city, taking pictures. But I don't do any of that anymore. I just... I don't trust myself to keep up with the game, or even act normal around them, you know? Speaking of chess, my friend Gary, he's got this beautiful wooden chess set. Hand-carved pieces from Poland or somewhere. The knights actually look like real horses, not just those blocky shapes you usually see. Gary's a bit of a fanatic, honestly. He watches all these grandmaster games on YouTube. He tried to teach me the Sicilian Defense once, but there are just too many variations. It’s like trying to memorize a phone book. Remember when they used to deliver those huge Yellow Pages to your door? They were so heavy, you could use them as a doorstop. My grandma used to keep one in her kitchen and she’d press flowers in it. She had this garden full of hydrangeas... but yeah, I just... I haven't been going to chess or doing much of anything. I just feel like I can't keep up.

doctor.intent: Assess the severity of functional impairment to distinguish between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Has your inability to focus and the mistakes you are making led to any formal disciplinary action or warnings from your supervisor at the hospital?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's mistakes at work have led to formal disciplinary action or warnings, which is not specifically covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't... I haven't been written up or anything like that. No formal warnings. Brenda, my supervisor, she's been pretty patient, I guess. She just kind of sighs and helps me fix whatever I messed up. She wears these reading glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck, so she's always pulling them up and dropping them back down when she looks at the clipboard. 

It actually reminds me of my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had a chain for her glasses too, but hers was made of fake pearls. She loved pearls. She even had a pearl steering wheel cover in her car. It was this huge boat of a Buick. I remember because she gave me a ride home once when I missed the bus. It was raining so hard that day, the streets were basically rivers, and that Buick just glided right through the puddles. My dad used to have a LeSabre, same kind of floaty suspension. You'd hit a bump and the car would just bounce up and down for a mile. He loved that car. He'd spend every Sunday waxing it in the driveway... but, um... no, Brenda hasn't called me into the office or given me any disciplinary papers.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing a marked decrease in functioning to differentiate between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) major depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Are you still able to carry out your work responsibilities to the same standard as you did before you started feeling this way, or would you say your ability to function at work is significantly impaired?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started making avoidable mistakes at work, needing coworkers to repeat simple requests, and avoiding chess nights and photography walks because I don’t trust myself to keep up or act normal.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about the patient's ability to function at work and whether it is significantly impaired, matching the Functional Impairment item.

patient.answer:
Well, no, definitely not to the same standard. It's... it's definitely impaired. Like I was saying, I'm making those avoidable mistakes, and I just can't seem to hold onto a thought. The nurses have to repeat simple requests two or three times before it clicks. It's like I'm moving through molasses. And it's not just work, it's everything. I've completely stopped going to chess nights, and I haven't taken my camera out for a walk in weeks. I just don't trust myself to keep up with the game or act normal around the guys. 

My camera is a Nikon, actually. I saved up for six months to buy it. It’s got this incredible zoom lens, you can see the craters on the moon if the night is clear enough. I used to love going down to the harbor at night to take long exposure shots of the boats. The water looks like glass when you do that. You have to use a tripod, though, otherwise the picture comes out all blurry. I bought a really sturdy carbon fiber one. It’s super light but it doesn't shake in the wind. The wind down by the harbor can get pretty intense, especially in November. It just whips right off the water. You have to wear layers. My mom used to knit these thick wool scarves... she made me this one that was dark green, forest green, I guess you'd call it. It was so warm, but it was incredibly itchy. I could only wear it over a turtleneck... but yeah, I just... I can't do my job the way I used to. I'm definitely not functioning like normal.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of functional impairment to differentiate between moderate (F32.1) and severe (F32.2) major depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Because you mentioned that you are still showing up to work and haven't received formal disciplinary action, would you say that you are still able to manage your basic daily self-care tasks, like showering, brushing your teeth, and keeping your home clean, or has your current state made even those simple things feel impossible?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's ability to manage basic daily self-care tasks (showering, brushing teeth, keeping the home clean), which is not explicitly covered in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I try to keep up with it, but honestly, it's getting harder. Some days I just look at the shower and it feels like... like climbing a mountain, you know? I haven't been doing laundry as much. The pile just sits there. It's mostly scrubs anyway. I have these blue scrubs, they’re the only color they let us wear on the floor. 

I used to have this pair of scrubs that were a slightly different shade of blue, like a navy, and Brenda actually pulled me aside and told me I couldn't wear them. It was a whole big thing. The hospital has a very strict dress code policy. They even dictate the color of our shoes. They have to be solid white or solid black, no logos. I bought these white clogs once, the kind the chefs wear? They are supposed to be slip-resistant. I slipped in the cafeteria anyway, right in front of the salad bar. Dropped a whole tray of jello. Red jello, cherry flavor. It went everywhere. The janitor, Frank, he was so mad. Frank’s been there for like thirty years. He has this massive ring of keys on his belt, it jingles every time he walks down the hall. It sounds like a sleigh is coming. My uncle used to dress up as Santa every Christmas and he had bells just like that... but, um... yeah, self-care is... it's slipping. I'm just so tired all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms cause significant functional impairment in social or occupational areas, which helps distinguish between F32.1 (moderate) and F32.2 (severe/with psychotic features or marked social/occupational impairment).
doctor.question: Given that you have stopped going to chess nights and taking your camera out, would you say that your symptoms have caused you to almost completely withdraw from your social life and personal interests?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to run in Van Cortlandt Park, take photos, and play chess with friends, but now I mostly tell myself there’s no point and end up sitting at home scrolling or checking my budget spreadsheet.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's withdrawal from social life and personal interests, which directly maps to the 'Loss of Interest' symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess you could say that. I just... I don't see the point anymore. Like I said, I stopped doing chess nights, and my camera is just gathering dust. I used to love running, too. I'd go for these long runs in Van Cortlandt Park. The trails there are really nice, especially in the fall when the leaves change. 

There's this one specific trail that loops around the back, near the old train tracks. They pulled the tracks up years ago, but you can still see the wooden ties rotting in the dirt. It's kind of sad, actually, thinking about how busy that train line used to be. My grandfather worked on the railroad, not that one, but out in Pennsylvania. He was a conductor. He had this beautiful pocket watch, gold plated, with an eagle engraved on the front. He used to let me hold it when I was a kid. It was so heavy in my hand. It ticked really loud, you could hear it from across the room if the house was quiet enough. The house was always quiet after my grandmother died. She used to bake these incredible apple pies, the whole house would smell like cinnamon and butter... 

But yeah, I don't run anymore. I just tell myself there's no point. I end up just sitting on my couch, scrolling on my phone or... or staring at my budget spreadsheet. Just looking at the numbers. It's all I seem to have the energy for.

inference.note: The patient's description of significant impairment in daily functioning, social withdrawal, psychomotor disturbance (either agitation or retardation), and the presence of cognitive symptoms ('cotton-brain') persisting for weeks without meeting criteria for mania or other conditions points to a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms.
